title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 96
paragraphs: Then, as more and more kept continually coming to him—because men learned that his decisions proved to be in accordance with the truth—Deioces, perceiving that everything was being referred to himself, would no longer sit in the place where he had formerly sat in public to judge cases, and said that he would judge cases no more, for it was not profitable for him to neglect his own affairs and to determine cases for his neighbors all day long. So then, since robbery and lawlessness prevailed in the villages even more than they did before, the Medes assembled together in one place and consulted with one another and discussed the state in which they were. And I suppose the friends of Deioces spoke much to this effect: “Seeing that we are not able to dwell in the land under the present order of things, let us set up a king from among ourselves; thus the land will be well governed and we ourselves shall be able to turn to our work, and not be ruined by lawlessness.” With words like these they persuaded themselves to have a king.
